metadata.title: HPSC FSO Unit 7 — Modern Food Packaging, Migration Regulations & Instrumental Food Analysis
metadata.source_basis: Grounded in the uploaded 81-page handout. Terminology, numerical values, statutory references, mechanisms and highlighted HPSC EXAM TRAP callouts are used as the primary basis.

exam_orientation.style: HPSC-oriented technical MCQ practice with single-best-answer items, plausible distractors, factual recall, mechanisms, applications, numerical values and regulatory interpretation.
exam_orientation.current_pattern_caveat: The handout's opening exam-strategy section describes an earlier objective/descriptive pattern. Publicly reported HPSC revision dated 16 October 2026 distinguishes a 100-question objective Screening Test (if held; General Studies/Haryana GK syllabus) from a 150-mark descriptive Subject Knowledge Test. This technical MCQ bank is therefore for technical recall and concept checking, not a claim that the current technical SKT is an MCQ paper.
exam_orientation.probability_note: No question bank can guarantee or reliably quantify the probability of an item appearing. The set prioritises high-yield concepts and explicit trap callouts in the uploaded handout.

structure.question_order: All questions and options appear first; no answers are shown in this section.
structure.answer_key_order: Consolidated answer key follows all questions.
structure.explanations_order: Detailed explanations for every question follow the complete answer key.

covered: solution–diffusion model and P = D × S
barrier paradox: polyolefins versus EVOH/nylon and PVDC
thin aluminium foil pinholes and lamination
active versus intelligent packaging; TTI versus freshness indicator
mercury cold-vapour AAS versus arsenic hydride-generation AAS
ash temperature and crude-fibre acid/alkali sequence
high_priority_exam_traps.emphasis: Highlighted HPSC EXAM TRAP callouts, statutory numbers, material/detector comparisons and procedural parameters receive deliberate weight.

metadata.source_limitations: Regulatory values and standards are reproduced as stated in the supplied handout; verify current amendments and official standards before enforcement use. Method-dependent values can vary with matrix and test conditions.

detailed_explanations.explanation: A permeant first dissolves in the polymer (solubility coefficient S), diffuses through it (diffusion coefficient D), and desorbs. Their product, P = D × S, governs steady-state permeation.
The permeant dissolves at the upstream surface, diffuses down its concentration gradient, and desorbs at the downstream surface.
Crystalline regions are largely impermeable. Higher crystallinity lengthens the path through the amorphous phase and reduces transmission; this helps explain HDPE's better barrier than LDPE.
PE and PP are hydrophobic and therefore resist water vapour, but their non-polar structures provide relatively poor oxygen barrier.
EVOH's hydroxyl-rich hydrogen-bonded structure gives exceptional dry oxygen barrier. Water plasticises this network, increasing free volume and oxygen transmission.
EVOH is hygroscopic. Hydrophobic PE or PP skins and tie layers protect it from moisture while retaining its exceptional oxygen barrier.
PVDC's high chlorine content and crystallinity give it excellent dual gas and moisture barrier, and its performance is comparatively stable with humidity.
Water vapour transmission rate is expressed as mass transmitted per unit area per day, commonly g/m²·day, under stated temperature and relative humidity.
EVOH's oxygen barrier is strongly humidity-dependent; its OTR may rise by an order of magnitude or more at high RH.
A thicker film gives a longer diffusion path, reducing steady-state transmission rate when material properties and other conditions are held constant.
Silica is the network former and forms about 70–74% of soda-lime container glass. Soda acts as a flux and lime as a stabiliser.
Soda lowers the melting temperature of silica-rich glass, improving manufacturability. Lime is added to stabilise the glass against water attack.
Borosilicate glass contains about 12% B₂O₃ and has a lower thermal expansion coefficient than soda-lime glass, so it tolerates larger temperature differentials.
Annealing near 550–600 °C allows locked-in stresses to relax; controlled slow cooling prevents residual stress and spontaneous breakage.
A polariscope (strain viewer) reveals stress patterns through optical effects in glass, helping assess annealing quality.
The FeSn₂ alloy layer forms during reflow and contributes to corrosion resistance between the steel base and free tin layer.
C-enamel contains zinc oxide. It reacts with H₂S to form white zinc sulfide, avoiding the black iron/tin sulfide staining that can occur in sulfur-rich foods.
R-enamel offers acid resistance and is used for fruit and tomato products. It is not the preferred coating for sulfur-bearing foods where C-enamel prevents black sulfide staining.
Thin foil is prone to pinholes caused by rolling inclusions and thin-gauge processing. Polymer layers bridge these defects in a laminate.
The common three-ply structure is PET outside for printability and strength, aluminium foil as barrier, and CPP inside as the heat-seal food-contact layer.
Cast polypropylene forms the inner food-contact sealant. It provides heat sealing and withstands retort temperatures of about 121–135 °C.
The pouch is typically only 15–25 mm thick, so its half-thickness is far less than the can's radial conduction distance. The cold spot heats sooner.
PVC and PVDC are distinct polymers. Plasticised PVC can contain mobile plasticisers, while PVDC's high chlorine content and crystallinity provide excellent oxygen and moisture barrier.
PVDC density is about 1.6–1.7 g/cm³, higher than PET, PVC and the polyolefins. This density makes it the densest common polymer in the comparison table.
PP has a density around 0.90–0.91 g/cm³, lower than LDPE/LLDPE and the other listed packaging polymers.
HDPE has little branching, allowing close chain packing and higher crystallinity. LDPE has extensive branching, reducing packing efficiency.
LLDPE has short-chain branches introduced by alpha-olefin comonomers such as butene, hexene or octene. It offers improved tensile, puncture and tear strength.
CPP is cast and unoriented, offering a soft, tough, heat-sealable layer that withstands retorting. BOPP is oriented and commonly used for outer packaging films.
Active packaging deliberately interacts, for example by absorbing oxygen or ethylene, releasing antimicrobial agents, or regulating moisture.
Intelligent packaging senses and reports information. It informs rather than deliberately changing the food environment.
A TTI reports the temperature history of a package and is therefore intelligent packaging. It does not itself remove oxygen or inhibit microbial growth.
An oxygen scavenger removes oxygen from the headspace or incoming permeant. Indicators and RFID tags communicate information and are intelligent packaging.
Reduced iron reacts with oxygen and water to form iron hydroxide/oxide products. The sachet consumes oxygen and lowers headspace oxygen concentration.
The stated stoichiometry is approximately 1 g iron for 300 mL oxygen at standard conditions, making iron sachets high-capacity scavengers.
The electrochemical rusting reaction requires water. Moisture-dependent systems therefore need sufficient water activity; self-reacting types carry their own moisture.
Iron is ferromagnetic and can be detected. Sachet insertion may need to occur after metal detection, or a non-metallic scavenger may be selected.
Silica gel is an amorphous porous adsorbent. Water molecules are physically adsorbed on its internal surface; it can be regenerated.
Molecular sieves are synthetic zeolites with defined pore sizes (e.g., 3A and 4A) that selectively adsorb water and can achieve very low humidity.
Potassium permanganate is a strong oxidant and toxic. It is immobilised on an inert carrier and kept physically separated from food.
Permanganate is reduced during ethylene oxidation, producing brown manganese dioxide (MnO₂), which signals exhaustion of the absorber.
1-MCP binds ethylene receptors and inhibits ethylene action. It is a gas treatment/ripening inhibitor, not a packaging absorber.
MAP establishes a selected gas mixture at the time of packaging. Controlled-atmosphere storage differs because gas composition is actively maintained during storage.
A freshness indicator may detect metabolites such as volatile amines or other spoilage markers. A TTI records time–temperature exposure, not actual microbial status.
Migration is transfer of constituents—monomers, additives, processing aids, NIAS, inks or adhesive components—from food-contact materials into food or simulants.
Higher temperature and longer contact time increase diffusion and migration. Fatty foods can also extract lipophilic migrants more effectively.
Printed surfaces can contact the food-contact side of adjacent packaging in reels or stacks, allowing ink components to transfer without direct food contact.
A functional barrier such as foil or sufficiently thick PET limits migration from underlying layers. The handout notes a no-carcinogen restriction; it is not a blanket exemption.
OM is a gravimetric measure of the total non-volatile material transferred, irrespective of chemical identity. It is a general inertness criterion.
SM is analyte-specific and compared with a substance-specific migration limit (SML), derived from toxicological considerations.
The handout states 60 mg/kg of food/simulant or 10 mg/dm² of contact surface under Schedule IV of the FSS (Packaging) Regulations, 2018.
Using the convention of 6 dm² packaging contact per kg food, 10 mg/dm² × 6 dm²/kg = 60 mg/kg.
OM and SM answer different questions. A material can pass the total-mass limit yet exceed the SML for a potent migrant such as a plasticiser or primary aromatic amine.
Simulant B is 3% acetic acid and represents acidic foods (pH below 4.5), such as fruit juices and pickles.
Simulant A is 10% ethanol and represents hydrophilic/aqueous foods with pH above 4.5. Remember that B, not A, is the acidic simulant.
D2 is the vegetable-oil simulant for fatty foods. Simulant E is a solid simulant for dry foods.
Simulant E is the solid simulant used for dry foods. The letter-based simulant mapping is a high-yield recall trap.
The handout gives an SML of 1.5 mg/kg for DEHP (bis(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate). Do not confuse this with the antimony SML.
Antimony is associated with PET polymerisation catalyst residues; the stated SML is 0.04 mg/kg. It must not be confused with the 1.5 mg/kg DEHP limit.
The handout records notification on 24 December 2018 and enforcement/effective date of 1 July 2019.
Schedule IV addresses plastics, listed Indian Standards and migration requirements. Schedule I covers paper/board, II glass and III metals/alloys.
IS 9845 is identified for overall migration testing. IS 9833 concerns pigments/colourants and IS 15495 printing inks for food packaging.
Components distribute differently between a stationary phase and a moving mobile phase, producing different migration/retention times.
The retention factor is adjusted retention time divided by hold-up time: k = (tR − t0)/t0.
Rs = 2(tR2 − tR1)/(W1 + W2). A value around 1.5 is conventionally taken as baseline separation for comparable peaks.
B/u represents longitudinal diffusion, which is more influential at low linear velocity. A is eddy diffusion and C·u is mass-transfer resistance.
Reversed-phase HPLC uses a non-polar bonded stationary phase such as C18 and a polar mobile phase of water with methanol or acetonitrile.
A stronger organic mobile phase competes more effectively with hydrophobic analytes for the non-polar stationary phase, reducing retention.
RID responds to refractive-index differences between eluent and reference. A gradient changes the eluent refractive index and causes baseline drift.
A photodiode-array/diode-array detector records multiple wavelengths across a spectrum, allowing comparison with characteristic absorption maxima and peak-purity checks.
Fluorescence detection is highly sensitive for naturally fluorescent compounds or derivatives. Aflatoxins B1 and G1 may need derivatisation to enhance fluorescence.
The handout explains that B1 and G1 fluoresce weakly in aqueous mobile phases; post-column bromination/iodination or other derivatisation enhances their fluorescence.
Simple sugars lack a strong UV-absorbing chromophore. RID can detect them, though it is less sensitive and generally requires isocratic elution.
Gas chromatography is suited to volatile and thermally stable analytes. Non-volatile, polar or thermolabile compounds are generally analysed by HPLC/LC-MS/MS.
FID produces ions from organic compounds in a hydrogen-air flame. It has a broad response to carbon-containing compounds and is destructive.
ECD responds strongly to compounds that capture electrons, especially halogenated pesticides. The handout identifies a ⁶³Ni beta source.
A ⁶³Ni beta source generates electrons in the detector. Electron-capturing analytes reduce the standing electron current.
Q1 selects the precursor ion, q2 is the collision cell where fragmentation occurs, and Q3 selects product ions. q2 is not a mass analyser.
MRM monitors defined precursor/product transitions by fixing Q1 and Q3. A quantifier and at least one qualifier transition support identification and confirmation.
Mercury is reduced to elemental vapour and measured by cold-vapour AAS at 253.7 nm. Arsenic/selenium use hydride generation; trace lead/cadmium require GFAAS or ICP-MS.
The six fractions are moisture, crude protein, crude fat/ether extract, total ash, crude fibre and nitrogen-free extract (NFE).
NFE is estimated by difference from 100 after subtracting the five measured fractions. Errors in those measurements accumulate in NFE.
The general factor 6.25 assumes protein contains about 16% nitrogen. Specific factors include 6.38 for milk and 5.70 for wheat in the handout.
The handout lists 6.38 for milk and 5.70 for wheat. These differ from the general factor 6.25.
Kjeldahl converts nitrogen to ammonium during digestion, releases ammonia on alkalisation and measures it by titration. Protein is then estimated using a conversion factor.
Kjeldahl measures nitrogen, not protein identity. Non-protein nitrogen such as urea, ammonium salts or melamine can raise the apparent protein estimate.
Sulfuric acid digests organic matter and converts amino nitrogen into ammonium sulfate. Catalysts accelerate digestion; potassium sulfate raises the boiling point.
K₂SO₄ raises the boiling point of the acid mixture, allowing digestion at a higher temperature and speeding oxidation.
Strong alkali converts ammonium ions into volatile ammonia, which is steam-distilled into a receiving solution.
Ammonia is trapped by boric acid; the borate-containing receiver is titrated with standard acid, commonly 0.1 N HCl. Alkali is used earlier to liberate ammonia.
Nitrogen (%) = [(Vsample − Vblank) × N × 1.4007] ÷ sample weight in grams. The factor incorporates the milliequivalent mass and percentage conversion.
The same nitrogen result is multiplied by different conversion factors. The handout's example gives about 9.02% using 6.25 and 8.22% using the wheat factor 5.70.
Solvent vapour condenses onto the sample in a thimble, dissolves lipid, and siphons back to the boiling flask when the chamber reaches the siphon level.
The handout identifies petroleum ether with a 40–60 °C boiling range for Soxhlet extraction. This is a solvent boiling range, not the furnace temperature.
Soxhlet commonly uses a non-polar solvent. Moisture impedes solvent access to lipid and can contaminate the extract, so the sample is dried and finely ground.
Both OM and SM criteria apply. Passing OM cannot offset an SML exceedance for an individual migrant such as DEHP.
The handout highlights GFAAS or ICP-MS for trace lead/cadmium. Flame AAS is generally insufficiently sensitive at these very low concentrations.
GC is suited to volatile and thermally stable analytes. Non-volatile, polar or thermolabile vitamins are more appropriately analysed by HPLC or LC-MS/MS.
C-enamel is formulated for sulfur-bearing foods; zinc oxide reacts with hydrogen sulfide to form white zinc sulfide rather than black iron/tin sulfide.
EVOH is humidity-sensitive. Coextruded skins protect the core; retort can cause temporary barrier loss ('retort shock') that may recover as the layer dries.
The handout identifies the use of newspaper and similar materials for food wrapping as prohibited. The example of snacks drained on newspaper is specifically flagged.
